claim: CRISPR/Cas9 technology has revolutionized genomic editing.
source: The CRISPR/Cas9 technology has revolutionized genomic editing (Cong et al., 2013; Doudna, 2020; Heidenreich and Zhang, 2016; Jinek et al., 2012; Mali et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published work on CRISPR/Cas9 technology.

claim: One major unresolved challenge is using CRISPR-based technologies to precisely and efficiently knock in large DNA fragments in somatic cells of living animals to label or modify endogenous proteins.
source: However, one of the major unresolved challenges is to use CRISPR-based technologies to precisely and efficiently knock in large DNA fragments in somatic cells of living animals (i.e., without generating transgenic animals) to label or modify endogenous proteins.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field, drawing on established knowledge of CRISPR limitations.

claim: Several studies have developed CRISPR/Cas9-based approaches to insert fluorescent protein-encoding sequences to label and visualize endogenous proteins in somatic cells.
source: Toward this goal, several studies have developed CRISPR/Cas9-based approaches to insert fluorescent protein (FP)-encoding sequences to label and visualize endogenous proteins in somatic cells, such as postmitotic neurons (Artegiani et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2019; Mikuni et al., 2016; Nakade et al., 2014; Nishiyama et al., 2017; Schmid-Burgk et al., 2016; Suzuki et al., 2016; Uemura et al., 2016; Willems et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Fluorescent visualization of proteins in living cells is essential for the mechanistic dissection of cellular and organismic processes.
source: Fluorescent visualization of proteins in living cells is essential for the mechanistic dissection of cellular and organismic processes because many functions of cells and organisms are established and manifested by their constituent proteins.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established scientific knowledge about the importance of protein visualization.

claim: Immunolabeling is typically incompatible with live imaging.
source: immunolabeling is typically incompatible with live imaging
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about immunolabeling techniques.

claim: Immunolabeling usually does not permit sparse labeling for cell-specific contrast in tissues.
source: it usually does not permit sparse labeling for cell-specific contrast in tissues.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about immunolabeling techniques.

claim: FP tagging typically involves overexpression, which may result in undesired off-target effects.
source: FP tagging typically involves overexpression, which may result in undesired off-target effects.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about FP tagging methods.

claim: Knock-ins of FP tags are costly and time-consuming in mammalian species.
source: Knock-ins of FP tags are costly and time-consuming in mammalian species
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about knock-in techniques.

claim: Knock-ins of FP tags are typically associated with poor contrast due to global expression of the FP-tagged protein of interest.
source: with the exception of certain complex schemes (e.g., Fortin et al., 2014; He and Huang, 2018), are typically associated with poor contrast due to global expression of the FP-tagged protein of interest (e.g., Herzog et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work.

claim: Current CRISPR-based somatic protein labeling technologies have moderate in vivo labeling efficiency, especially for large DNA insertions required for FP labeling (~15% or less).
source: First, the in vivo labeling efficiency is moderate, especially for the large DNA insertions required for FP labeling (~15% or less) (Mikuni et al., 2016; Nishiyama et al., 2017; Suzuki et al., 2016; Uemura et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work reporting labeling efficiencies.

claim: Current CRISPR-based methods that target protein coding sequences or their immediately adjacent exonic sequences are error-prone.
source: Second, and more importantly, these methods, which target protein coding sequences or their immediately adjacent exonic sequences, are error-prone.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discussion of NHEJ pathway and INDELs in the context of existing methods.

claim: Prime editing only nicks the DNA and has started to make precise insertion of short (<50 bp) DNA sequences possible.
source: The precise insertion of short (<50 bp) DNA sequences has started to become possible via prime editing (Anzalone et al., 2019), which only nicks the DNA
evidence: Supported by citation to published work on prime editing.

claim: Insertion of larger DNA fragments still requires the generation of double-stranded DNA breaks (DSBs).
source: however, the insertion of larger DNA fragments still requires the generation of double-stranded DNA breaks (DSBs).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about DNA editing mechanisms.

claim: The efficient non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) pathway often results in unwanted insertions/deletions (INDELs) that cause mutations and/or frame shifts at edited loci involving DSBs.
source: At the edited loci involving DSBs, including those loci where the DNA insertion does not occur, the efficient non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) pathway often results in unwanted insertions/deletions (INDELs) that cause mutations and/or frame shifts (Cong et al., 2013; Doudna, 2020; Heidenreich and Zhang, 2016; Mali et al., 2013) (see also Figure 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to figures showing INDEL events.

claim: INDELs occur regardless of whether NHEJ or homologous-dependent repair (HDR) is engaged for the insertion process.
source: This is the case regardless of whether NHEJ or homologous-dependent repair (HDR) is engaged for the insertion process (Roberts et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work.

claim: Reversible DNA editing may allow for great flexibility in both research and gene therapy.
source: Finally, it has been increasingly recognized that reversible DNA editing may allow for great flexibility in both research and gene therapy (Nakamura et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to published work.

claim: The inserted labels using existing approaches are not readily removable at a later time.
source: however, the inserted labels are not readily removable at a later time using existing approaches.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discussion of existing methods and their limitations.

claim: CRISPIE allows for the nearly error-free insertion of FP sequences with high efficiency.
source: Here, we present a strategy, called CRISPR-mediated insertion of exon (CRISPIE), which allows for the nearly error-free insertion of FP sequences with high efficiency.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper, supported by data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: CRISPIE targets introns and inserts a designer donor module, which includes an exon encoding the desired protein sequence and the surrounding intronic sequences.
source: Instead of targeting gene exons, CRISPIE targets introns and inserts a designer donor module, which includes an exon encoding the desired protein sequence and the surrounding intronic sequences.
evidence: This describes the method design.

claim: INDELs occurring at the insertion junction within the intronic region of DNA will be spliced out, resulting in very low error rates at the mRNA level (>98% correct).
source: INDELs occurring at the insertion junction within the intronic region of DNA will be spliced out (Figure 1A), resulting in very low error rates at the mRNA level (>98% correct).
evidence: Supported by data presented in the manuscript and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: CRISPIE is flexible and broadly compatible with both N- and C-terminal labeling.
source: CRISPIE is flexible and broadly compatible with: (1) both N- and C-terminal labeling
evidence: Supported by data showing labeling at both termini.

claim: CRISPIE is compatible with proteins with diverse structures and functions, including pre- and post-synaptic proteins and cytoskeletal proteins.
source: (2) proteins with diverse structures and functions, including pre- and post-synaptic proteins and cytoskeletal proteins
evidence: Supported by data showing labeling of multiple protein types.

claim: CRISPIE is compatible with all major transfection methods.
source: (3) all major transfection methods
evidence: Supported by data showing successful transfection using multiple methods.

claim: CRISPIE is compatible with FPs with diverse colors.
source: (4) FPs with diverse colors
evidence: Supported by data showing labeling with different colored FPs.

claim: CRISPIE is compatible with multiple animal species.
source: (5) multiple animal species.
evidence: Supported by data showing labeling in human, mouse, and rat cells/tissues.

claim: Introns offer ample editing sites to choose from.
source: In part because introns offer ample editing sites to choose from
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about intron structure and variability.

claim: INDELs at the DNA level do not affect the success of editing in CRISPIE.
source: and because INDELs at the DNA level do not affect the success of editing
evidence: This is supported by data showing high mRNA fidelity despite DNA-level INDELs.

claim: A high labeling efficiency (up to 43%) was achieved in cortical neurons of living mice using CRISPIE.
source: a high labeling efficiency (up to 43%) was achieved in cortical neurons of living mice.
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: CRISPIE-mediated DNA insertions are erasable.
source: Importantly, CRISPIE-mediated DNA insertions are erasable.
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 6.

claim: By flanking the donor module with additional designer CRISPR editing sites in the intronic region, the inserted DNA fragment can be erased at a later time.
source: By flanking the donor module with additional designer CRISPR editing sites in the intronic region, the inserted DNA fragment can be erased at a later time.
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 6.

claim: CRISPIE may allow for the routine labeling of proteins at endogenous levels.
source: CRISPIE may allow for the routine labeling of proteins at endogenous levels
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential applications of CRISPIE.

claim: CRISPIE can be expanded to the insertion of other genetically encoded functional sequences to manipulate protein function.
source: and can be expanded to the insertion of other genetically encoded functional sequences to manipulate protein function.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential applications of CRISPIE.

claim: Human β-actin (ACTB) was labeled at its N-terminus with monomeric EGFP (mEGFP) in human U2OS cells.
source: As a proof of principle, we first labeled human β-actin (ACTB) at its N-terminus with monomeric EGFP (mEGFP) in human U2OS cells
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The sgRNA/SpCas9 complex cuts an editing site at the first intron of ACTB.
source: The sgRNA/SpCas9 complex cuts an editing site at the first intron of ACTB (Figure 1C), as selected using the BROAD Institute sgRNA designer (Doench et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1C and citation to sgRNA design tool.

claim: The released donor module is inserted into the cut site at the ACTB intron via the NHEJ pathway.
source: The released module is then inserted into the cut site at the ACTB intron via the NHEJ pathway.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about NHEJ-mediated DNA insertion.

claim: The module-flanking sgRNA-targeted sequences are in the reverse orientation to facilitate the insertion of the module in the forward orientation.
source: The module-flanking sgRNA-targeted sequences are in the reverse orientation to facilitate the insertion of the module in the forward orientation (Suzuki et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work.

claim: The donor module includes an exon in the appropriate translational phase (0–0 for intron 1 of ACTB) encoding mEGFP and peptide linkers.
source: The donor module includes an exon in the appropriate translational phase (0–0 for intron 1 of ACTB) encoding mEGFP and peptide linkers (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3B1.

claim: At the exon-intron junctions, ~100 bp of intronic sequence and ~10 bp of adjacent exonic sequence were taken from an obligatory intron and its adjacent exons of mouse CaMKIIα (Camk2a).
source: At the exon-intron junctions, ~100 bp of intronic sequence and ~10 bp of adjacent exonic sequence were taken from an obligatory intron (i.e., no reported alternative splicing events) and its adjacent exons of mouse CaMKIIα (Camk2a), a highly expressed protein in the brain, to include the splicing donor or acceptor site (Wang and Burge, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work on splicing sites.

claim: mEGFP labeling was observed at 3–4 days post-transfection.
source: mEGFP labeling was observed at 3–4 days post-transfection (Figure 1D)
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: mEGFP labeling required the presence of both sgRNA/SpCas9 and the donor module.
source: and required the presence of both sgRNA/SpCas9 and the donor module.
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1D showing no labeling without sgRNA.

claim: Over 35% (37 ± 5%) of transfected cells were mEGFP-labeled.
source: Over 35% (37 ± 5%) of transfected cells, as identified by the expression of mRuby3 (red), were mEGFP (green)-labeled (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: The 37 ± 5% labeling efficiency likely represents a lower bound because the co-transfection rate of all three plasmids is unlikely to reach 100%.
source: This likely represents a lower bound of labeling efficiency, since the co-transfection rate of all three plasmids is unlikely to reach 100%.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design and transfection efficiency considerations.

claim: Confocal and super-resolution structured illumination microscopy (SIM) revealed that the mEGFP signals exhibited the characteristic distribution of actin protein.
source: Confocal and super-resolution structured illumination microscopy (SIM) revealed that the mEGFP signals exhibited the characteristic distribution of actin protein (Fischer et al., 1998; Planchon et al., 2011; Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1F and citations to published work on actin distribution.

claim: Time-lapse confocal microscopy revealed dynamic actin ruffles at the edges of cells.
source: Time-lapse confocal microscopy revealed dynamic actin ruffles at the edges of cells (Figure 1G), which is consistent with the current knowledge of actin dynamics (Fischer et al., 1998; Planchon et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1G and citations to published work on actin dynamics.

claim: Cells with CRISPIEd actin grew at a rate indistinguishable from that of unlabeled cells in the same dish.
source: Furthermore, cells with CRISPIEd actin grew at a rate indistinguishable from that of unlabeled cells in the same dish (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The results are consistent with the predictions for a functional, FP-labeled endogenous actin protein.
source: These results are consistent with the predictions for a functional, FP-labeled endogenous actin protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed actin distribution, dynamics, and cell growth.

claim: Bands corresponding to the successful insertion (i.e., insertion in the forward orientation) at the targeted site are observed in green-labeled cells for both the genomic DNA and the mRNA.
source: As expected, bands corresponding to the successful insertion (i.e., insertion in the forward orientation) at the targeted site are observed in green-labeled cells for both the genomic DNA and the mRNA (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Systematic analyses of green-labeled cells detected all possible editing events at the genomic DNA level, including no label insertion, forward insertion, and inverted insertion.
source: Systematic analyses of green-labeled cells detected all possible editing events at the genomic DNA level, including no label insertion, forward insertion, and inverted insertion (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Insertion events were typically non-homologous (i.e., both chromosomes differentially edited).
source: indicating that insertion events were typically non-homologous (i.e., both chromosomes differentially edited).
evidence: This is an inference based on the detection of multiple editing events in the same cells.

claim: An inverted label insertion would inevitably cause disruptive mutations if the coding sequence had been targeted.
source: Had the coding sequence been targeted, an inverted label insertion would inevitably cause disruptive mutations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the understanding of how inverted insertions affect coding sequences.

claim: Because the donor only contained the splicing signals for exon inclusion in the forward orientation, only wild-type and forwardly inserted mRNAs were detected.
source: However, under our conditions, because the donor only contained the splicing signals for exon inclusion in the forward orientation, only wild-type and forwardly inserted mRNAs were detected (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: At the genomic DNA level in red-only cells, over 70% (834/1181 reads) of PCR amplicon sequences contained INDELs.
source: Remarkably, at the genomic DNA level in red-only cells, over 70% (834/1181 reads) of PCR amplicon sequences contained INDELs (Figure 2C, and second column of Figure 2D)
evidence: Supported by NGS data presented in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: At the mRNA level in red-only cells, 99.7% (2930/2936 reads) of the sequences did not contain INDELs (p<0.001, cf. genomic DNA).
source: In contrast, at the mRNA level in these cells, 99.7% (2930/2936 reads) of the sequences did not contain INDELs (p<0.001, cf. genomic DNA) (Figure 2D, second column)
evidence: Supported by NGS data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: The mRNA INDEL rate in red-only cells was no different from control, untransfected cells (99.7%, 5761/5771 reads).
source: which was no different from control, untransfected cells (99.7%, 5761/5771 reads) (Figure 2D, first column).
evidence: Supported by NGS data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: Undesired INDELs were frequently detected in all sequenced amplicons from green cells at the genomic DNA level.
source: Similarly, undesired INDELs were frequently detected in all sequenced amplicons from green cells at the genomic DNA level (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by NGS data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: Similar high rates of INDELs were observed at the genomic DNA level in other insertion locations of ACTB and in another gene (TUBA1B) across two different cell lines.
source: Similar high rates of INDELs were also observed at the genomic DNA level in other insertion locations of ACTB and in another gene (TUBA1B) across two different cell lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by NGS data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Few errors were detected at the mRNA level (INDELs 24–87% for DNA vs. 0.3–2% for mRNA).
source: However, few errors were detected at the mRNA level (INDELs 24–87% for DNA vs. 0.3–2% for mRNA; Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by NGS data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: The correct-to-mutation ratios for mRNA are 50- to 300-fold, which are around two orders of magnitude higher than those for DNA.
source: These numbers correspond to correct-to-mutation ratios of 50- to 300-fold for mRNA, which are around two orders of magnitude higher than those for DNA.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the NGS data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: Although inverted insertion and INDEL events may occur at the DNA level, CRISPIE is resistant to these disruptive events at the mRNA level.
source: These results demonstrate that, although inverted insertion and INDEL events may occur at the DNA level—which would have caused mutations or frame shifts when using existing strategies to target coding sequences—CRISPIE is resistant to these disruptive events at the mRNA level.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the NGS data presented in Figure 2.

claim: For insertion strategies that target coding sequences, the options for targeting sites are limited.
source: For insertion strategies that target coding sequences, the options for targeting sites are limited
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about coding sequence structure and constraints.

claim: Not all potential targeting sites allow for high-efficiency editing.
source: and not all potential targeting sites allow for high-efficiency editing (Doench et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work on sgRNA efficiency.

claim: INDELs cause mutations or frame shifts when targeting coding sequences, thereby reducing the likelihood of successful labeling.
source: Furthermore, as discussed above, INDELs cause mutations or frame shifts, thereby reducing the likelihood of successful labeling.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the effects of INDELs in coding sequences.

claim: CRISPIE is insensitive to INDELs.
source: In contrast, CRISPIE is insensitive to INDELs
evidence: Supported by data showing high mRNA fidelity despite DNA-level INDELs.

claim: The lengths of introns usually offer ample choices for potential targeting sites.
source: and the lengths of introns usually offer ample choices for potential targeting sites.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about intron structure and variability.

claim: CRISPIE may have the potential to achieve higher labeling efficiency than strategies that target coding sequences.
source: CRISPIE may therefore have the potential to achieve higher labeling efficiency than strategies that target coding sequences.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the advantages of CRISPIE.

claim: Five different editing sites (i1 to i5) were selected using the BROAD Institute sgRNA designer (with Azimuth v2.0 scores of 0.57–0.69).
source: Five different editing sites (i1 to i5 in Figure 3A) were selected using the BROAD Institute sgRNA designer (with Azimuth v2.0 scores of 0.57–0.69) (Doench et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 3A and citation to sgRNA design tool.

claim: All five sites permitted the successful labeling of ACTB.
source: we found that all five sites permitted the successful labeling of ACTB
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: The labeling efficiencies varied significantly across the five sites, with the highest labeling efficiency corresponding to around 20-fold of the lowest.
source: however, the labeling efficiencies varied significantly (Figure 3B), with the highest labeling efficiency corresponding to around 20-fold of the lowest.
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: There are only two possible SpCas9 editing sites around the start codon of ACTB (referred to as e1 and e2).
source: There are only two possible SpCas9 editing sites around the start codon of ACTB (referred to as e1 and e2; Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Both exonic sites exhibited significantly lower labeling efficiencies compared to the optimized CRISPIE editing (greater than fivefold).
source: Despite using their optimal insertion donors (for both, see Figure 1—figure supplement 3B6), both exonic sites exhibited significantly lower labeling efficiencies compared to the optimized CRISPIE editing (greater than fivefold; Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Between the e1 and e2 sites, the one with the higher Azimuth score was in fact less efficient (Azimuth scores = 0.55 and 0.62, respectively).
source: Between the e1 and e2 sites, the one with the higher Azimuth score was in fact less efficient (Azimuth scores = 0.55 and 0.62, respectively)
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: The labeling efficiency is not yet entirely predictable.
source: indicating that the labeling efficiency is not yet entirely predictable.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Azimuth scores do not perfectly predict labeling efficiency.

claim: CRISPIE allows for systematic optimization by screening for highly efficient editing sites.
source: Nevertheless, CRISPIE allows for systematic optimization by screening for highly efficient editing sites
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that different intronic sites have different efficiencies.

claim: When optimized, CRISPIE can achieve higher labeling efficiency than exonic editing.
source: and, when optimized, can achieve higher labeling efficiency than exonic editing.
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: The CRISPIE method should be broadly applicable for use with different FPs or with other functional domains, different protein targets, and different animal species.
source: The CRISPIE method should be broadly applicable for use with different FPs or with other functional domains, different protein targets, and different animal species.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential applications of CRISPIE, which is then tested in the following experiments.

claim: ACTB was successfully labeled in U2OS cells using cyan (mTurquoise2), green-yellow (mNeonGreen), and red (mRuby3) FPs.
source: To test different FP labels for potential multiplex imaging studies, we successfully labeled ACTB in U2OS cells using cyan (mTurquoise2), green-yellow (mNeonGreen), and red (mRuby3) FPs (Figure 4A, donor plasmids illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B2-4).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: When both mTurquoise2 and mNeonGreen donors were included simultaneously, double-labeled cells could be found.
source: Notably, when both mTurquoise2 and mNeonGreen donors were included simultaneously, double-labeled cells could be found, which appeared to be capable of dividing (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: FP labeling does not affect cell viability in diploid CRISPIEd cells.
source: indicating that FP labeling does not affect cell viability in diploid CRISPIEd cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that double-labeled cells can divide.

claim: Microtubules, mitochondria, focal adhesion complexes, and the endoplasmic reticulum were successfully labeled in U2OS cells by labeling tubulin alpha 1B (TUBA1B), translocase of outer mitochondrial membrane 20 (TOMM20), vinculin (VCL), and calreticulin (CALR), respectively.
source: To test the applicability of CRISPIE to different protein targets, we labeled several additional important subcellular structures in U2OS cells, namely microtubules, mitochondria, focal adhesion complexes, and the endoplasmic reticulum, by labeling tubulin alpha 1B (TUBA1B), translocase of outer mitochondrial membrane 20 (TOMM20), vinculin (VCL), and calreticulin (CALR), respectively (Figure 4B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B; Lam et al., 2012; Rizzo et al., 2009; Roberts et al., 2017; Shroff et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 4B and citations to published work on these proteins.

claim: Cells with CRISPIEd TUBA1B grew at a rate indistinguishable from that of unlabeled cells in the same dish.
source: In a growth test, cells with CRISPIEd TUBA1B grew at a rate indistinguishable from that of unlabeled cells in the same dish (Figure 1—figure supplement 4)
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: CRISPIEd TUBA1B is functional.
source: suggesting that such labeled TUBA1B is functional.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that cells with CRISPIEd TUBA1B grow normally.

claim: The TOMM20 and VCL genes were labeled at their respective last introns.
source: Notably, the TOMM20 and VCL genes were labeled at their respective last introns (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: TOMM20 and VCL encoded proteins are best tagged at their C-termini.
source: because their encoded proteins are best tagged at their C-termini (Rizzo et al., 2009; Roberts et al., 2017; Shroff et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work.

claim: CRISPIE is readily compatible with C-terminal labeling.
source: This demonstrates that CRISPIE is also readily compatible with C-terminal labeling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the successful C-terminal labeling of TOMM20 and VCL.

claim: For VCL, the coding sequence of the last exon was included in the insertion donor sequence, and a stop codon was introduced at the end of the mEGFP coding sequence.
source: For some genes, such as VCL, there are coding sequences of significant lengths present at the last exon, downstream of the possible CRISPIE labeling site. To prevent potential disruption of protein function caused by an insertion in the middle of the protein, the coding sequence of the last exon of VCL was included in the insertion donor sequence, and a stop codon was introduced at the end of the mEGFP coding sequence (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: β-actin (Actb) was successfully labeled in mouse Neuro 2A cells.
source: To test the applicability in different animal species, we further labeled β-actin (Actb) in mouse Neuro 2A cells.
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: A mouse-specific sgRNA was used because introns are degenerative across species.
source: A mouse-specific sgRNA was used because introns are degenerative across species (e.g., see Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing sequence divergence.

claim: The labeling was successful and was dependent on the correct combination of the species and the corresponding sgRNA.
source: The labeling was successful and was dependent on the correct combination of the species and the corresponding sgRNA (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: CRISPIE labeling was successful in rat neurons.
source: CRISPIE labeling was also successful in rat neurons (Figure 5A, see below).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: CRISPIE is versatile and readily applicable to many different FP labels, protein species, and animal species, and can be used to tag proteins at their N- and C-termini.
source: Overall, these results indicate that CRISPIE is versatile and readily applicable to many different FP labels, protein species, and animal species, and can be used to tag proteins at their N- and C-termini.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The biolistic method was used to deliver the sgRNA and donor for rat β-actin (rActb), and the cytosolic marker mRuby3, to cultured rat hippocampal slices.
source: First, we used the biolistic method (i.e., 'gene gun') to deliver the sgRNA and donor for rat β-actin (rActb), and the cytosolic marker mRuby3, to cultured rat hippocampal slices.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: CRISPR-based labeling has not yet been demonstrated using the biolistic method, likely due in part to the relatively low labeling efficiencies.
source: Notably, although the biolistic transfection method is widely used in studying the cellular functions of neurons, CRISPR-based labeling has not yet been demonstrated using this method, likely due in part to the relatively low labeling efficiencies.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the literature and the limitations of existing methods.

claim: High-contrast double labeling—for example, the target protein together with a cell morphology marker—in brain tissue remains challenging.
source: For this same reason, high-contrast double labeling—for example, the target protein together with a cell morphology marker—in brain tissue remains challenging.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the limitations of existing methods.

claim: 6–45 neurons were transfected per brain slice, as determined by their red mRuby3 fluorescence.
source: In our experiments, 6–45 neurons were transfected per brain slice, as determined by their red mRuby3 fluorescence.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental results.

claim: On average 15% (15 ± 4%, n = 6 slices) of transfected neurons exhibited successful labeling of actin.
source: Among them, on average 15% (15 ± 4%, n = 6 slices) exhibited successful labeling of actin (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: In some slices, as many as six to seven successfully labeled neurons of different neuronal types, including dentate gyrus neurons, CA1 and CA3 pyramidal neurons, and interneurons, could be detected.
source: In some slices, as many as six to seven successfully labeled neurons of different neuronal types, including dentate gyrus neurons, CA1 and CA3 pyramidal neurons, and interneurons, could be detected (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Glial cells could also be labeled.
source: Glial cells could also be labeled (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The labeled neurons exhibited normal miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) in frequency and amplitude when compared to adjacent untransfected neurons.
source: The labeled neurons exhibited normal miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) in frequency and amplitude when compared to adjacent untransfected neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: CRISPIE provides a viable option for protein labeling using gene gun in cultured slices.
source: These results indicate that CRISPIE provides a viable option for protein labeling using gene gun in cultured slices.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and 2.

claim: Similar results were obtained in cultured mouse hippocampal slices from an SpCas9 heterozygous genetic background, which constitutively expresses SpCas9.
source: Similar results were obtained in cultured mouse hippocampal slices from an SpCas9 heterozygous genetic background, which constitutively expresses SpCas9 and thereby simplified the experimental design (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Other synaptic proteins, including synapsin (SYN1), tubulin (TUBA1B), and CaMKIIα, were also successfully labeled.
source: Other synaptic proteins, including synapsin (SYN1), tubulin (TUBA1B), and CaMKIIα, were also successfully labeled (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 5A and B.

claim: In many labeled cells, both the mRuby3 cytosolic marker and mEGFP were readily detectible.
source: In many labeled cells, both the mRuby3 cytosolic marker and mEGFP were readily detectible
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: The three proteins—β-actin, α-tubulin 1B, and CaMKIIα—exhibited distinct subcellular distributions: actin was highly enriched in dendritic spines, and CaMKIIα was moderately enriched, whereas tubulin was excluded from spines.
source: By quantifying their distribution between the dendrites and spines using a previously described spine enrichment index (SEI) (Zhong et al., 2009), we found that the three proteins exhibited distinct subcellular distributions: actin was highly enriched in dendritic spines, and CaMKIIα was moderately enriched, whereas tubulin was excluded from spines (Figure 5C; see Materials and methods for quantification details).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 5C and citation to published method.

claim: In utero electroporation (IUE) was used to introduce the sgRNA, the donor, and the cytosolic marker mRuby3 into the somatosensory cortex of SpCas9 mice to label β-actin or tubulin in separate experiments.
source: To determine whether CRISPIE can be used to label endogenous proteins in vivo, in utero electroporation (IUE) was used to introduce the sgRNA, the donor, and the cytosolic marker mRuby3 into the somatosensory cortex of SpCas9 mice to label β-actin or tubulin in separate experiments (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: Among the transfected red cells, the labeling efficiencies were 43 ± 5% for actin and 30 ± 5% for tubulin.
source: Among the transfected red cells, the labeling efficiencies were 43 ± 5% for actin and 30 ± 5% for tubulin (Figure 5E)
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: The labeling efficiencies of 43 ± 5% for actin and 30 ± 5% for tubulin are both significantly higher than previously reported for CRISPR-based endogenous labeling of any protein in vivo.
source: both of which are significantly higher than previously reported for CRISPR-based endogenous labeling of any protein in vivo (Mikuni et al., 2016; Nishiyama et al., 2017; Suzuki et al., 2016; Uemura et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by comparison to published work.

claim: This high level of labeling efficiency allowed routine in vivo imaging in the brains of living mice.
source: This high level of labeling efficiency allowed us to routinely perform in vivo imaging in the brains of living mice (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: An adeno-associated virus (AAV) harboring the sgRNA targeting β-actin, the donor, and mRuby3 was generated.
source: Finally, as viruses have become an increasingly prevalent method of transfection, we generated an adeno-associated virus (AAV) harboring the sgRNA targeting β-actin, the donor, and mRuby3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: When injected into the cortex of SpCas9 mice, this virus successfully transduced neurons in vivo and labeled the actin cytoskeleton.
source: When injected into the cortex of SpCas9 mice, this virus successfully transduced neurons in vivo and labeled the actin cytoskeleton (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 5G.

claim: CRISPIE can be readily applied using a variety of widely used methods to transfect neurons both in vitro and in vivo with high efficiency.
source: Overall, CRISPIE can be readily applied using a variety of widely used methods to transfect neurons both in vitro and in vivo with high efficiency.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Reversible gene editing may offer significant benefits in research, and in gene therapy in the future.
source: Reversible gene editing may offer significant benefits in research, and in gene therapy in the future.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential benefits of reversible gene editing.

claim: Existing CRISPR-based methods for endogenous labeling and large-fragment DNA insertions are not readily reversible.
source: However, existing CRISPR-based methods for endogenous labeling and large-fragment DNA insertions are not readily reversible.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of existing methods and their limitations.

claim: CRISPIE allows for the inclusion of functional elements at the flanking intronic regions of the donor module without affecting the mRNA.
source: CRISPIE allows for the inclusion of functional elements at the flanking intronic regions of the donor module without affecting the mRNA.
evidence: This is based on the design of CRISPIE and the understanding of RNA splicing.

claim: Additional designer sgRNA targeting sequences (DRS-1) were included at both ends of the module to allow for later excision of the inserted module.
source: Taking advantage of this, we included additional designer sgRNA targeting sequences (DRS-1; Gao et al., 2019) at both ends of the module (Figure 6A). These added sites allowed for the later excision of the inserted module guided by the DRS-1 sgRNA.
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 6A and citation to published work.

claim: A U2OS cell clone of CRISPIEd ACTB was isolated, and all cells derived from this clone uniformly exhibited green-labeled actin structures.
source: To demonstrate this reversibility, we isolated a U2OS cell clone of CRISPIEd ACTB. All cells derived from this clone uniformly exhibited green-labeled actin structures (Figure 6B, left panel).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: When DRS-1 sgRNA and SpCas9 were co-transfected with the transfection marker mRuby3, the green label was absent or greatly attenuated in over three quarters (76 ± 6%) of the mRuby3-positive cells at 5 days after transfection.
source: When DRS-1 sgRNA and SpCas9 were co-transfected with the transfection marker mRuby3, the green label was absent or greatly attenuated in over three quarters (76 ± 6%) of the mRuby3-positive cells at 5 days after transfection (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Transfection with an sgRNA targeting mouse β-actin did not result in detectible change in the green labeling.
source: As a control, transfection with an sgRNA targeting mouse β-actin did not result in detectible change in the green labeling
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 6B and C.

claim: CRISPIE is a readily reversible gene editing approach at the DNA level.
source: indicating that CRISPIE is a readily reversible gene editing approach at the DNA level.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Several studies have developed CRISPR/Cas9-based approaches to insert fluorescent protein (FP)-encoding sequences to label and visualize endogenous proteins in somatic cells, such as postmitotic neurons.
source: Toward this goal, several studies have developed CRISPR/Cas9-based approaches to insert fluorescent protein (FP)-encoding sequences to label and visualize endogenous proteins in somatic cells, such as postmitotic neurons (Artegiani et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2019; Mikuni et al., 2016; Nakade et al., 2014; Nishiyama et al., 2017; Schmid-Burgk et al., 2016; Suzuki et al., 2016; Uemura et al., 2016; Willems et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Intronic editing has been used to introduce non-coding DNA tags, microRNAs, gene disruptions, exon replacements, and super-exons.
source: While intronic editing has been used to introduce non-coding DNA tags, microRNAs, gene disruptions, exon replacements, and super-exons (Bednarski et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2018; Jarvik et al., 1996; Lee et al., 2018; Li et al., 2016; Miura et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to published work.

claim: Previous intronic editing studies involved cloning of the cell or organism.
source: these studies involved cloning of the cell or organism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discussion of prior intronic editing studies.

claim: CRISPIE can conceivably be used when cloning of the edited cell or organism is involved.
source: Although CRISPIE can conceivably be used when cloning of the edited cell or organism is involved
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential applications of CRISPIE.

claim: CRISPIE's strength lies in its applicability to somatic cells.
source: its strength lies in its applicability to somatic cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discussion of CRISPIE's advantages.

claim: Somatic cell editing offers significant advantages compared to cloning-based approaches, including lower cost, faster turnaround time, and potentially controllable alterations in labeling density.
source: Somatic cell editing offers significant advantages compared to cloning-based approaches, including lower cost, faster turnaround time, and potentially controllable alterations in labeling density.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the advantages of somatic cell editing.

claim: Sparse labeling is desired for high-contrast imaging, whereas high-density labeling is needed for biochemical or proteomic analyses.
source: In particular, with regard to labeling density, sparse labeling is desired for high-contrast imaging, whereas high-density labeling is needed for biochemical or proteomic analyses.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the requirements for different types of experiments.

claim: Somatic cell editing will be required under most circumstances when gene editing is applied directly on patients for therapeutic purposes.
source: In addition, somatic cell editing will be required under most circumstances when gene editing is applied directly on patients for therapeutic purposes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about gene therapy approaches.

claim: Several previous studies have labeled endogenous proteins in somatic cells.
source: As mentioned earlier, several previous studies have labeled endogenous proteins in somatic cells (Gao et al., 2019; Mikuni et al., 2016; Nishiyama et al., 2017; Schmid-Burgk et al., 2016; Suzuki et al., 2016; Uemura et al., 2016; Willems et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work.

claim: Previous methods that directly target exons are sensitive to INDELs.
source: However, these methods are sensitive to INDELs because they directly target exons.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the effects of INDELs in exons.

claim: When previous methods are applied in vivo, the majority of transfected cells are not labeled (labeling efficiency ≤15%), but INDELs can still occur and cause major disruption of the targeted protein in these unlabeled cells.
source: Notably, when these methods are applied in vivo, the majority of transfected cells are not labeled (labeling efficiency ≤15%), but INDELs can still occur and cause major disruption of the targeted protein in these unlabeled cells.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the limitations of existing methods and the effects of INDELs.

claim: In the (v)SLENDR approach, the sequences within a short range before the start codon or after the stop codon can be used as target sites, thereby alleviating the side effects of INDELs.
source: In the (v)SLENDR approach (Mikuni et al., 2016; Nishiyama et al., 2017), which engages HDR as the insertion mechanism, the sequences within a short range before the start codon or after the stop codon can be used as target sites, thereby alleviating the side effects of INDELs.
evidence: Supported by citations to published work on (v)SLENDR.

claim: INDELs often include deletions tens of base pairs or longer.
source: However, INDELs often include deletions tens of base pairs or longer (e.g., Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: For many genes, INDELs in the 5' and 3' untranslated regions may potentially affect the trafficking, stability, or translational control of the mRNA.
source: For many genes, INDELs in the 5' and 3' untranslated regions may potentially affect the trafficking, stability, or translational control of the mRNA (Fortin et al., 2014; Goldie and Cairns, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work.

claim: HDR occurs with low efficiency in non-dividing cells.
source: Furthermore, HDR occurs with low efficiency in non-dividing cells.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about HDR efficiency.

claim: The vSLENDR approach increases HDR efficiency in postmitotic neurons using high-titer AAV.
source: The vSLENDR approach increases HDR efficiency in postmitotic neurons using high-titer AAV
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the vSLENDR method.

claim: AAV construction and generation add significantly to the cost and time of experiment.
source: however, AAV construction and generation add significantly to the cost and time of experiment
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about AAV production.

claim: The in vivo labeling efficiency of vSLENDR remains low (≤15%).
source: and the in vivo labeling efficiency remains low (≤15%).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the vSLENDR method's efficiency.

claim: The recently developed prime editing technique, while exhibiting high precision, can only insert short sequences (<50 bp) and has not been demonstrated in vivo.
source: Finally, the recently developed prime editing technique, while exhibiting high precision, can only insert short sequences (<50 bp) and has not been demonstrated in vivo.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the prime editing method and its limitations.

claim: Compared to previous methods, CRISPIE is nearly error-free in both labeled cells, and transfected but unlabeled cells.
source: Compared to previous methods, CRISPIE is nearly error-free in both labeled cells, and transfected but unlabeled cells.
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 2.

claim: CRISPIE is broadly compatible in vitro and in vivo with all tested transfection methods, including liposome-based transfection, biolistic transfection, in utero electroporation, and viral infection.
source: It is broadly compatible in vitro and in vivo with all tested transfection methods, including liposome-based transfection, biolistic transfection, in utero electroporation, and viral infection.
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figures 1, 4, and 5.

claim: CRISPIE exhibits approximately fivefold higher labeling efficiency in side-by-side comparisons with an exon targeting strategy.
source: CRISPIE exhibits approximately fivefold higher labeling efficiency in side-by-side comparisons with an exon targeting strategy
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: CRISPIE achieves up to 2.7-fold higher efficiency than the best in vivo labeling efficiency described in the literature.
source: and achieves up to 2.7-fold higher efficiency than the best in vivo labeling efficiency described in the literature (Nishiyama et al., 2017; Suzuki et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by comparison to published work.

claim: This higher labeling efficiency is significant as it greatly increases the feasibility of in vivo multiplexed imaging of the labeled protein with the cellular context revealed by a cytosolic marker.
source: This higher labeling efficiency is significant as it greatly increases the feasibility of in vivo multiplexed imaging of the labeled protein with the cellular context revealed by a cytosolic marker (e.g., Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 5F.

claim: The higher labeling efficiency provides a new starting point for further improving the labeling efficiency toward 100%, which may be required for future therapeutic purposes.
source: It also provides a new starting point for further improving the labeling efficiency toward 100%, which may be required for future therapeutic purposes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential for future improvements.

claim: CRISPIE is limited by the availability of introns at or near the desired targeting sites.
source: CRISPIE is limited by the availability of introns at or near the desired targeting sites.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of CRISPIE.

claim: Such sites are available in the genes of a large number of protein species for labeling at either the N- or C-termini.
source: However, as demonstrated, such sites are available in the genes of a large number of protein species for labeling at either the N- or C-termini.
evidence: Supported by data showing labeling of multiple proteins at both termini.

claim: Labeling at an internal site of a gene is feasible as long as the insertion does not disrupt the function of the encoded protein.
source: In addition, labeling at an internal site of a gene is feasible as long as the insertion does not disrupt the function of the encoded protein.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential applications of CRISPIE.

claim: Many introns reside at the junctions of functional domains because introns have evolved in part to facilitate functional domain exchanges.
source: Many introns reside at the junctions of functional domains because introns have evolved in part to facilitate functional domain exchanges (Kaessmann et al., 2002; Patthy, 1999).

source: These junctions may serve as candidate internal insertion sites for FP labeling.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential applications of CRISPIE.

claim: Although CRISPIE improves upon the precision at the target site, it does not prevent potential off-target cleavages of sgRNA/Cas9.
source: At the same time, although CRISPIE improves upon the precision at the target site, it does not prevent potential off-target cleavages of sgRNA/Cas9.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of CRISPIE.

claim: Increasingly powerful bioinformatics tools allow for the selection of targeting sites with less likely off-target effects.
source: However, increasingly powerful bioinformatics tools allow for the selection of targeting sites with less likely off-target effects (e.g., Doench et al., 2014; Doench et al., 2016)

claim: This concern will be further alleviated or eliminated in the future by the continued development of high-fidelity Cas9 variants.

claim: Although CRISPIE enables the tagging of endogenous proteins with low error rates, it does not ensure that the tagged protein functions the same as the wild-type protein.
source: Similarly, although CRISPIE enables the tagging of endogenous proteins with low error rates, it does not ensure that the tagged protein functions the same as the wild-type protein.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of CRISPIE.

claim: Not all tagging is benign, and rigorous characterization will be needed for each tagging experiment.
source: Not all tagging is benign, and rigorous characterization will be needed for each tagging experiment.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about protein tagging.

claim: When designing the donor template, care should be given to not create unintended splicing acceptor sites in the inverted orientation.
source: It should also be noted that, when designing the donor template, care should be given to not create unintended splicing acceptor sites in the inverted orientation.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the understanding of RNA splicing.

claim: Inverted insertion events can cause mutations at the mRNA and protein levels if unintended splicing acceptor sites are created.
source: Otherwise, inverted insertion events can cause mutations at the mRNA and protein levels.
evidence: This is based on the understanding of RNA splicing and the effects of inverted insertions.

claim: CRISPIE-based DNA insertion can be readily erased.
source: CRISPIE-based DNA insertion can be readily erased

claim: CRISPIE-based DNA insertion erasure offers flexibility in both research studies and gene therapy in the future.
source: which offers flexibility in both research studies and gene therapy in the future.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential benefits of reversible gene editing.

claim: Although the original editing site will be destroyed during the labeling-erasing cycle, adjacent editing sites within the intron can allow for additional rounds of labeling, thereby simulating a reversible process.
source: Although the original editing site will be destroyed during the labeling-erasing cycle, adjacent editing sites within the intron can allow for additional rounds of labeling, thereby simulating a reversible process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the understanding of CRISPIE and the availability of multiple intronic sites.

claim: CRISPIE can label endogenous proteins with high fidelity, high efficiency, and reversibility in diverse animal species.
source: Overall, CRISPIE can label endogenous proteins with high fidelity, high efficiency, and reversibility in diverse animal species.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the paper.

claim: This method can also conceivably be used to introduce other functional domains to modify protein function for research and for therapeutic purposes.
source: This method can also conceivably be used to introduce other functional domains to modify protein function for research and for therapeutic purposes.

claim: Introns are often poorly conserved and tolerate stochastic mutations better than exons.
source: Because introns are spliced out of mRNAs, they are often poorly conserved and tolerate stochastic mutations better than exons (e.g., see Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
